newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's Iliescu vows moderation at campaign end.
newsitem.headline: Romania's Iliescu vows moderation at campaign end.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu urged Romania's voters to endorse what he said was a moderate approach to reform by re-electing him on Sunday, seven years after he helped to overthrow communist rule.

At the official end of campaigning in bitterly-contested elections, opinion polls suggested Iliescu had about 32 percent of the vote, only four points ahead of his closest rival, and a run-off ballot seemed certain.
Iliescu said Romania had to avoid the abrupt lurches he said were being offered by other presidential candidates who denounce him as a leftover of the communist system.

"Romania needs no violent ruptures to destroy the delicate balance in society. It needs basic, accelerated change," he said an impassioned plea during a televised debate on Thursday attended by all 16 presidential candidates,

"We cannot turn Romania into a testing ground. I have remained an honest man close to the masses, close to their worries and needs. My message to you is: Let us continue together what we started in the revolution."

Iliescu has led Romania, only east European state where former communists have enjoyed uninterrupted power, since the December 1989 revolt that toppled dictator Nicolae Ceausescu. He won earlier elections in 1990 and 1992.

The two candidates given a chance of ousting him, academic Emil Constantinescu and former prime minister Petre Roman, say he has been timid and slow with reforms and has created mass poverty. Living standards have fallen further behind those in Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

"The president keeps telling us that nothing can be done. We're here to prove that isn't so," Constantinescu told viewers. "The people running this country seem to think that national interests are different from those of each citizen."
The television programme was the first head-to-head meeting between the three main contenders, but it was blunted by rules forbidding any direct exchanges between them.

The broadcast turned into a string of monologues by some presidential no-hopers, including a faith healer who says he has cured five million people, a priest who runs a soup kitchen and the leaders of the car owners' and pensioners' parties.

The six-week campaign has seem ample mud-slinging, with particularly vicious attacks launched in video clips, and Iliescu, even if he wins re-election, is likely to face a hostile government and parliament.

His Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), also in power since 1989, trails Constantinescu's Democratic Convention in parliamentary pollls also taking place on Sunday. Tough talks on forming a government coalition are certain to follow.

The major opposition groupings say they will have nothing to do with Iliescu's PDSR and have formed a tactical alliance to guard against what they fear will be an attempt at mass vote-rigging. But they have also spent much of the campaign attacking each other.
